summary: A guide to how the IETF works, written for newcomers attending its meetings. It is part of the FYI series and is informational. It was replaced by RFC 3160.

eli5.summary: A friendly handbook for first-time visitors to a big club of internet engineers.

subtitle: An updated guide for newcomers to the IETF meetings and organization.

tldr.problem: New IETF meeting attendees need a practical guide to understand the organization, prepare for meetings, and participate effectively.
tldr.mechanism: This updated FYI document provides an accessible introduction to the IETF's structure, mission, meeting logistics, preparation strategies, and resources. It includes updates reflecting changes in the IETF since 1993.
tldr.outcome: Newcomers are better prepared to contribute to IETF work and navigate meetings productively. This document is now also available online, and later versions include web references.

today: RFC 1718 is an Informational FYI document published in November 1994 that has been superseded by RFC 3160. It reflects the IETF structure and meeting practices as they evolved from 1993 to 1994, including additions like IPv6/IPng area and online proceedings availability.

sections.title: What is the IETF
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is a loosely self-organized group of engineers and researchers making technical contributions to the engineering and evolution of the Internet and its technologies. It is the principal body developing new Internet standard specifications. The IETF's mission includes identifying and proposing solutions to pressing Internet problems, specifying protocols and architecture, making recommendations about standardization to the IESG, facilitating technology transfer from the IRTF, and providing a forum for information exchange among vendors, users, researchers, and network managers.

The IETF is not a traditional standards organization and has no official membership. Anyone may register for and attend meetings. The closest equivalent to membership is being on IETF or working group mailing lists, where the best information about current activities is found. The IETF meets three times a year and is made up of volunteers who fulfill the IETF mission.
sections.eli5: The IETF is a group of engineers who volunteer to improve the Internet. It is not a company—anyone can join and attend meetings. The real work happens three times a year when people meet, and in between through mailing lists.

sections.title: Structure and Organization
sections.content:
The IETF operates within a larger organizational framework. The Internet Society (ISOC) is a professional society overseeing Internet growth and evolution. The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) is a technical advisory group chartered to provide oversight of Internet architecture and protocols. The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) is responsible for technical management of IETF activities and the Internet standards process.

The IETF is divided into eight functional areas: Applications, Internet, Network Management, Operational Requirements, Routing, Security, Transport, and User Services. Each area has one or two area directors. Area directors, along with the IETF/IESG Chair, form the IESG.

Within each area are Working Groups, which are groups of people working under a charter to achieve specific goals such as creating protocols, informational documents, or resolving Internet problems. Birds of a Feather (BOF) sessions are informal meetings held once or twice to determine if enough interest exists to form a working group. Working group members are people on that group's mailing list, though anyone may attend meetings.
sections.eli5: The Internet Society is the top organization. Below it are advisory groups (IAB and IESG) that make decisions. The IETF splits into eight areas, each with directors. Inside are working groups of people solving specific problems. BOFs are informal meetings to test interest in new topics.

sections.title: Meeting Logistics and Participation
sections.content:
To attend an IETF meeting, you must register and pay a registration fee. Early registration, ending about one month before the meeting, costs less than late registration. Registered attendees receive a packet with an orientation sheet, the at-a-glance logistics sheet (showing room assignments and maps), a list of working group acronyms, the latest agenda, and a name tag.

Newcomers should attend the Newcomers' Orientation, held on Sunday afternoon before the registration reception. It covers what is in the attendee packets, the meaning of colored dots on name tags (blue for working group/BOF chairs, green for local hosts, red for IAB members, yellow for IESG members), and how to read the at-a-glance sheet. The orientation also explains the IETF structure and standards process.

The opening plenary on Monday morning is the most heavily attended session and provides important introductory remarks. The agenda is fluid and updated multiple times; always check the at-a-glance sheet first, then the bulletin board near the registration desk for room changes. An IETF social event is traditionally held during each meeting for informal networking. Dress code is casual—'dress for the weather' is the standard rule.
sections.eli5: Sign up and pay to attend. You get a packet with maps and schedules. Attend the newcomer orientation on Sunday to understand how things work. The agenda changes often, so always check the bulletin board. There is a social event for meeting other attendees.

sections.title: Being Prepared and Using Resources
sections.content:
Preparation is essential for productive participation. Before attending, read documents that working group and BOF chairs distribute, follow discussions on relevant mailing lists, or review archived messages. The more work done on mailing lists before the meeting, the less time the meeting needs to spend on foundational discussion.

Join the IETF announcement mailing list (send a request to ietf-announce-request@cnri.reston.va.us) for all meeting information and announcements. You may also join the IETF discussion list (ietf@cnri.reston.va.us) for technical discussions. Always send subscription requests to the '-request' addresses, never to the main lists. Most working groups have their own mailing lists.

Working groups progress through phases: initial phase (ideas welcome), development phase (solution chosen), and final phase (refinement). Reopening decided issues is considered bad form. The InterNIC archives contain working group documents starting about one month before each meeting; these should be reviewed by attendees planning to participate in those working groups.
sections.eli5: Read the documents and follow mailing lists before the meeting. Use '-request' addresses to join, not the main lists. Working groups move through phases—understand the current phase before suggesting changes.

sections.title: RFCs, Drafts, and Meeting Proceedings
sections.content:
RFCs (Requests for Comments) are the formal publication series for Internet technical documents. They may specify protocols, describe information, or provide operational guidance. The FYI subseries documents overviews and introductory topics, while the STD subseries identifies RFCs that specify Internet standards. When an RFC is revised, it receives a new RFC number, but FYI and STD numbers remain constant for stable reference.

Internet-Drafts are working documents of the IETF valid for six months. Any group or individual may submit one for distribution. Internet-Drafts may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted at any time and should not be cited as archived materials or standards.

IETF Proceedings are compiled two months after each meeting and sent to attendees. They include the final agenda, IETF overview, IESG report, area and working group reports, technical presentation slides, and the attendee list. Proceedings are also available online via Gopher, WorldWide Web, and anonymous FTP to encourage use of Internet technology itself.
sections.eli5: RFCs are official Internet documents. FYIs are introductions. STDs are standards. Internet-Drafts are temporary working papers. After each meeting, Proceedings are published with all the presentations and discussions.
